segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Back on one of the early episodes of our radio show, I had my friend Vertamae Grosvenor come on. Verta was this amazing cook. She wrote a cookbook in 1970, Vibration Cooking, that is still in print today. And Verta had this story that she would tell sometimes that, back when her book was published, she was interviewed on the Today show by Barbara Walters, who was on the show back then.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the way Verta told this story, she's on TV, making fried chicken for Barbara Walters. And at some point, Barbara Walters asked her, how do you tell the chicken's done? And Verta says, you can tell by the sound. And in Verta's telling, Ms. Walters gives her this skeptical look, like, give me a break, and cuts to commercial. Verta said that was always people's reaction.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: They say, you're crazy, Verta. That's not it. They said, tell me something real, like, what is it? 15 minutes, 20 minutes, or whatever. And I say, you've got to listen to the sound of the grease. Listen to the music.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So for years, Vertamae claimed that you can tell if a chicken's done purely by the sound. And to prove the point, she agreed to come onto our radio show to conduct this little radio experiment, where my co-workers and I fried a chicken. and we recorded it at four different stages of frying, and then shuffled the order of the recordings to play for Verta to demonstrate, once and for all, was it true? Can somebody tell if a chicken's cooked without any visual clues, without smell?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, and so here is me playing the four recordings for Verta and her trying to pick out which one is the chicken when it's finished.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Let's roll. And our listeners at home can play along with us here. Let's roll the first little sample sound.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [SIZZLING]

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: I would say--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah?

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: I'd say that's something like the middle.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. But that definitely isn't towards the end, you're saying.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Yeah, it's in the middle going toward the end. It's in the 3/4 part.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, let's hear sound number two, please.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [FASTER SIZZLING]

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Number two is toward the end, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, number three.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [HARSH SIZZLING]

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: I think that's the beginning, more toward the beginning.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That is more toward the beginning. And number four?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [SLOWER SIZZLING]

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: That's an ender. That's toward the end.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When all those little balls are forming on the bottom, those little, nice, crusty--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, Verta, if you would have to hazard a guess as to which one would be the very last one--

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: I'd still say it's one or two that's toward the end.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The answer is number two, so Vertamae came reasonably close. But she was not totally certain. Telling if a chicken is done only by sound turned out to be harder than she thought it to be.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Yes, it was hard. You have to see it. Do you know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Oh, it's a serious-- it's a labor-intensive thing. You've got to stay on it. You just can't be talking on the phone and watching TV. You got to stay on that chicken.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I was asking your daughters today, and they were saying how they can also tell if rice is done by the sound.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Oh, yeah, that's true. Yeah, I taught them that. Those are the kind of family values I taught my children. Listen to the sound of the chicken.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: You know? Listen to the sound of the rice.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Vertamae died four years ago. And so I have to say, it got to me a little, listening to this next part of the interview where she talks about her daughters, and how happy it made her to hear what they said about her.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: You talked to both of them?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I talked to both of them.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They were both really funny. One of them said, "Everything that she cooks is golden brown and perfect, perfect, perfect."

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Who said that?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I believe it was Chandra.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But she said, "But just because we're her daughters, that doesn't mean that she tells us the real recipes. We ask her for the recipes and she tells us recipes. But then when we cook them, they're not the same, and we know that she's holding back on ingredients."

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Well, that's not quite true. But you know--

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: Well, now, I just tell them. But then they have to find out the rest for themselves.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There you go.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: You see what I'm saying?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As with so many things in parenting.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: I say, I put a little ginger in. Now, I'm not going-- then they have to figure out how much a little ginger is.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Vertamae Grosvenor
segments.text: That's what they have to do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Food, of course, really is everything. It's family, and it's culture, and it's tradition. It's improvisation and it's art. And today on our show, for Thanksgiving weekend, we put together a show made of stories we've done over the years about food. In every one of these stories, somebody heads out on a quest, either to figure something out or to do something very differently with food than most of us do. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, "Dead Ringer." So a few years back, one of our producers, Ben Calhoun, set out on a mission much more eccentric and labor-intensive than figuring out if a chicken is done by listening to the sound. Here he is.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I first heard about this whole thing in an email. It came from a listener, a woman named Emily Rancer. She works in the food industry. And the letter Emily wrote was about a story she'd heard from a farmer. The farmer who told her this is apparently a person of some standing in the pork industry. And admittedly, I don't know the first thing about the pork industry. But he's in charge of a pork-producing operation that spans several states.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: The story he told Emily went something like this. A while ago, he was visiting a pork processing plant in Oklahoma. He's walking through it with a friend, a guy who managed the plant, actually. And at some point, he saw boxes stacked on the floor labeled, artificial calamari. He stood there, wondering for a second. And then he asked his friend, what's artificial calamari? Bung, his friend replied. It's hog rectum, rectum that would be sliced into rings, deep fried, and boom, there you have it.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: OK, if I can, let me just narrate for you what this would mean. It would mean that in restaurants everywhere, right this second, people are squeezing lemon wedges over crispy, golden rings and dipping the rings into marinara sauce, and they're eating hog rectum. Now they're chewing, satisfied and deeply clueless. It's payback. It's payback for our blissful ignorance about where our food comes from and how it gets to us. It's amazing, and it's perfect.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But it also seems like it couldn't possibly be true. So I called up the farmer to talk to him personally, I wanted to hear it firsthand. And the farmer confirmed the story, the entire thing-- the boxes, the bung. But when I asked him to go on the record, to tape an interview and give his name here on the radio, he very politely declined, which seems suspicious, right? When I asked him why, he said he'd spoken with his girlfriend about it, and she suggested that he should think about the words that he wanted to come up when somebody googled his name.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: This was all fine, though, because he referred me to the real expert, the guy who gave him the tour of the hog processing plant. And that guy, he agreed to talk.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: [PHONE RINGS]

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Hi. Is this Ron?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Yeah, this is Ron Meek, meat processing plant manager, presently residing in Mountain View, Missouri, where he runs an organic beef processing plant there called Beyond Organic. If the story really were true, Ron would have been the guy who explained to the farmer what was in those boxes.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: The boxes are 10-pound boxes. And they were all-- they cut off so much, like, maybe a 10 or 12-inch piece of the bung. And you know what it looks like? This looks like-- after they're cleaned, and washed, and everything, they just look like a bunch of big noodles in a box is all it looks like.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But specifically, the labels that said "imitation calamari," where did you personally see the imitation calamari labels?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Oh, I've never seen a label say that. That's all I was told by the people that told me that. The people I worked for, they told me that.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Oh, the people that you worked for told you that it was used for imitation calamari?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: And is there any possibility that you think that when they were explaining this to you that they were kind of having you on a little bit?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Having me on?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Yeah, like--

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Bull-[BLEEP] me?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Well, I wouldn't think that. But you know, it could be 5%. It could have been that, you know? But I seriously doubt it.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: OK, just to give a little better picture, a pork bung-- and bung is the actual industry term for it-- is long, and floppy, and ugly. At one end, it widens out into this more bulbous shape, like a pink, wrinkly pear. That's the rectum. At the other end, it narrows into a soft, pinkish-white tube. I know. It sounds gross.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But also, consider we are a nation that eats more than a billion pounds of sausage every year-- billion, with a B. Maybe you like liverwurst, or capicola, or summer sausage with a natural casing. Then you, like me, have eaten bung-- stuffed, dried bung. A lot of brats and Italian sausages are stuffed in intestine. So if you eat those regularly, you pretty much live up the street from bung.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So why does the idea of a fried ring of bung just feel grosser? Well, partly, it's the visual, right? When you see that little ring of calamari, you don't want to picture it in the context of a pig's behind. Then there are all the people who don't eat pork, period. Ron said there's also another reason.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Just because of the word bung, probably. People don't just want to jump up and say, man, I'm going to eat me some bung tonight. That's just the way it is.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But the big question, the question you've been thinking about since we got on this topic, have you or I eaten imitation calamari, bung dressed up as seafood? Well, Ron didn't know. He said his plant exported a lot of their bung to Asia. But he just didn't know much about whatever happened after it left the door, so he could only speculate. Anything, he said, would be a wild guess.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So I turned to people who would know. Is pork bung being falsely peddled as calamari? I called the USDA. The USDA's food inspection service issued the following statement to me. "Products we inspect, including those derived from pork, must be accurately labeled and cannot purport to be a product of another species."

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So it's against the rules, but people break the rules. A recent study of seafood by a group called Oceana used DNA testing and found that all across the country, fish is regularly being labeled as other species in restaurants and in grocery stores-- escolar sold as white tuna, Pacific rockfish being fraudulently sold as snapper.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: In Miami, more than 30% of fish was being sold as something it wasn't. In New York, the number was 39%. Boston, 48%. Los Angeles-- are you ready? 55%. 55%. That means if you order fish in LA, you are most likely eating a species you did not order.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: In other words, seafood substitution is rampant in this country. And depending on where you live, from what I can tell, you can get cleaned hog bung for about half the price of clean squid. So there would be money in it, if you could pull off the switch. And as best as I can tell, were you to do this, you would not be caught.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: A lawyer who's familiar with this area of law and regulation told me, once bung leaves the plant, there is a variety of agencies and entities that would be in play-- USDA, FDA, state and local government. But ultimately, he said, the regulation we have is not designed to catch an offense like this. It's aimed mostly at sanitation and food safety. So bottom line, the lawyer said, if somebody wanted to do it, chances are they'd get away with it.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So is someone out there doing this? Well, for weeks, I looked for an answer. The USDA says they've never heard of anyone trying to pass pork bung as squid or any other species.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: [PHONE RINGS]

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I contacted the National Restaurant Association, the National Pork Producers Council, the National Pork Board--

segments.speaker: Receptionist 1
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: --a squid fishermen's association--

segments.speaker: Receptionist 2
segments.text: Good afternoon, National Pork Board.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: --Sysco and other big food and restaurant supply companies.

segments.speaker: Diane Pleschner-steele
segments.text: It's hog what?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Bung. Hog rectum.

segments.speaker: Diane Pleschner-steele
segments.text: Oh my gosh.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: That's the executive director of the California Wetfish Producers Association. But the answer was pretty much always the same, nobody had heard of it. But almost to a person, they added that that doesn't mean it's not happening somewhere.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Ron Meeks said a lot of the bung from his plant got exported. So my next call was to the US Meat Export Federation, which confirmed that, quote, "The main destinations for pork bungs are China, Hong Kong, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, and the Philippines. They are mainly used for processing, but we are aware of some uses in soups and certain entrees. We are not aware of them being used as a substitute for calamari, but it's not impossible," unquote.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So over the past few weeks, I've called Asian food suppliers, people who live in, work in, and eat in those countries. I talked to a woman named Corinne Trang, who's written an overarching compendium of Asian cuisines. I've talked to academics at NYU, and Haverford, and USC, and Harvard. I've reached out to chefs who know Asian food. The answer, again, always similar-- never heard of it, but it's possible, partly because bung doesn't have such a complicated reputation in Asia where it has to be some kind of secret ingredient, like it does here.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: On the other hand, though, people pointed out that in Korea and Japan, you can't get more than a few hours from the ocean. Squid is cheap and it's readily available. You'd only eat a substitute if you wanted the substitute. Generally, people said, if the switch was happening somewhere, they guessed China.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Eventually, I found my way to this guy who I was really excited about, someone who I thought might have my answer. He was-- get this-- an anthropologist who lived and worked in China for 40 years where he studied food, and specifically, meat. When I talked to him, though, he made two points.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Point one, my question about this happening in Asia was racist. Even just asking the question was racist because it plays on ignorant stereotypes about other cultures eating things that we perceive as weird.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Point two was that Ron Meek, my guy from the pig plant, Ron was pulling my leg. And he was getting away with it because I was a dumbass. He told me more than once that I should, quote, "find something worthwhile to do with myself." When we ended our conversation, he told me that he was refusing to even dignify what I was doing by appearing on the radio or by letting me use his name.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: OK, so to respond to his points one by one, first, am I racist against Asians? Well, I'm half-Chinese. My mom's Chinese. Like anyone, I've had the occasional issue with my mother, but this has not been one of them. We grew up eating chicken feet and fish eyes, and I think it's possible to raise the question of who eats what without being racist.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: His second point, though, that Ron Meek was pulling my leg-- the guy was still an expert on meat in China. So I called Ron back.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: All right, shoot me some questions, dude.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I told him the whole thing, about the anthropologist, about what he said.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I guess, the only thing I want to ask you is are you messing with me?

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: No. That was what my boss told me. I was like, what the hell do we save these hog bungs for? He says, they use them for imitation squid and stuff like that.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But so in your heart of hearts, you believe it.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Yeah, man. I ain't going to set here and tell you things that are bull-[BLEEP] and play with you when I'm just going off of my knowledge of saving hog bungs. You got to think about how far advanced slaughterhouses are, especially big ones, that want to make every penny count.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: Like the one I worked at, you bring the pigs in. You stun them, then you stick them. And the blood goes off into a trough. And it goes down, and it's vacuum sucked out of there with a vacuum into centrifuges. And they separate the blood from the blood plasma.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Ron Meek
segments.text: And they save that. They save the lungs. They save the pancreas. They save the spleens. They save the hearts. The only thing left, by the time it's all said and done, is a skull and jaw bones. You can be an anthropologist all you want. If you don't work in a processing plant, you don't know [BLEEP].

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I contacted the plant Ron worked at where this happened. And for what it's worth, they backed him up. They said their sales team had heard of people eating pork bung as imitation calamari, though they hadn't witnessed it firsthand or heard it directly from a customer. It was all hearsay.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So at the end of all this, I still had no proof that anyone was passing off bung as squid. Then I realized, I hadn't asked the more basic question here. Could bung do it? Could it pass as calamari?

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: And that question led me to a guy named Eddie Lin. Eddie Lin has eaten a lot of bung. At least a hundred times, he said, probably more. Eddie has an extreme food blog called Deep End Dining and an online TV show called Kamikaze Kitchen.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: I could definitely see a resemblance texturewise.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, definitely. They're sort of a rubbery texture, sort of like a calamari.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Huh.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: But you would really have to get rid of that, needless to say, foul flavor and odor from the bung.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Somehow, I hadn't figured that the bung, once it was scrubbed, and rinsed, and cleaned with steam, that it would still taste like-- you know.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: So yeah, you would definitely have to do some major, major blanching [LAUGHS] or brining. I meant brining, yeah.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Mhm. Just to try to leach those flavors out of there.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: Yeah, those flavors have been marinating in that pig for quite a while, so--

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: A lifetime.

segments.speaker: Eddie Lin
segments.text: Yeah. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: He thought it wouldn't be easy, but he thought it could be done. And there was only one way to tell if he was right, to cook up some bung and eat it. And if the taste was overwhelming and the texture was all wrong, well, then I'd have my answer. And at this point-- I'll be frank-- I started to root for the bung.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: I realized that this is not a story about fraud. It's not a bait-and-switch story. It's a story about possibility. It's classic rags-to-riches. It's about whether a cut of meat, perhaps the lowliest, most malignable cut of meat in America, might somehow, in at least one place on the planet, be dipped in the redemptive oils of the great culinary equalizer that is the deep fryer.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: And it might emerge transformed, no longer an outcast, but instead, hair combed, clean shaven, in a suit and tie, it might walk reborn onto a table. Through shear force of resemblance, it might be loved. Its history, years of drudgery and hardship, doing the body's least glamorous job all washed away.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: No, this is not the story of a conman like Bernie Madoff. It's Pretty Woman. This is whether Goodwill Hunting finds his way out of Southie. It's whether Charlie, on that very last chocolate bar, really can get a golden ticket.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: To do all this, to try it, I called my little sister, Lauren. She's a chef, trained abroad at the Cordon Bleu. Worked at Michelin star restaurants. She's that kind of chef. Soon, we were standing in front of a deli case. And I don't know why I feel hesitant about saying this, because I don't think it's racist. It was in Chinatown.

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: Pork bung, there it is. Look at it. It looks like the sphincter.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Wait. What do you mean it looks like a--

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: This one up here that's cut up, it looks like a butt hole. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: It does.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And Lauren had theories about pulling it off-- brining, soaking, maybe braising. But once we got to the store, once she'd seen the meat up close, her doubts got worse.

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: I think after looking at it, I don't think that-- I don't think it's going to--

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: You don't think it's going to work.

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: No. It's too thick. There's too much-- there's too much, like, muscle tissue. It's too thick. You'd have to use a ring cutter to make it the right thickness.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: What do you think those bits are in there?

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: Oh, you know, poo.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: My sister said Eddie Lin was definitely right. The giveaway would be the stubborn flavor of poo. That flavor, she said, it's tough to get rid of. The Earth revolves around the Sun, and bung will always taste like [BLEEP].

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: But there was no backing out now. We would eat. We would eat our way to the truth. And so what if it didn't look good? So what if bung was destined to taste like bung? You know who it didn't look good for, and he still put up a fight? Rocky Balboa, that's who. This was it, the bung versus calamari, squid versus tail, the rumble in the bung hole.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: We set up the tasting at a restaurant, in the lull between lunch and dinner. In the dining room, there was just a few tables eating. And all around the restaurant, the morning shift was wrapping up as we walked in with a red cooler filled with squid and hog bung.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So originally, I'd recruited some half a dozen people from our office at This American Life as tasters. The final group the day of the tasting included, from the office, Seth Lind and Brian Reed.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: So when's the last time that you guys had calamari?

segments.speaker: Seth Lind
segments.text: I had calamari probably like a month ago.

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: And what about you, Brian?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I haven't had it since we got this tip about the possible--

segments.speaker: Ben Calhoun
segments.text: Oh, my gosh. Have you been avoiding?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Yeah, no, totally. And to be honest, I ate calamari pretty-- I'm a regular eater of calamari. Not like all the time. But it's something I'll routinely order if it's on an appetizer menu. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So Jonathan Gold was a kind of legendary food writer, invented this way of writing about restaurants that treated hole-in-the-wall places and street food with the same seriousness that other restaurant critics had always written about fancy places. segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And before he died in 2018, Jonathan was on our show a couple times. It ended with him talking about-- I don't even know how exactly what to call it-- but the nature of eating. But it began with Jonathan explaining to me how he ended up living with a chicken. He explained that that happened by accident. When he was in his 20s, he was not living the kind of life one usually associates with chickens.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: This was during the period when I considered myself to be a performance artist of sort-- a naked performance artist, to be specific.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: I don't know if you've been to a lot of performance art, but this was sort of really typical of the stuff that was going on in the period. And I showed up. And I was naked. And I was carrying a machete. And I was blindfolded.

segments.text: And I stood in the middle of this pile of supermarket chickens, like the broilers that you buy. And the chicken that I had bought was tethered to a 3-foot rope around me. And I hacked up and down blindly with a machete.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.text: You've done your wad. You've done your sort of bid for art, which has either worked, or it hasn't. But you're sitting there. You're covered with chicken eflluvia, in my case. It stinks to high hell. Everybody's gone. And you've got to clean up. And you're naked.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And in doing that, he stumbled across that thin, thin line that separates food items on the one hand from pets on the other, that divides the animals we eat from the animals we love.

segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.text: The fact is, we need food to be just food. segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: Exactly. Could I tell you a short-- a small story?

segments.text: A few weeks ago, I was in this Korean restaurant in Koreatown in Los Angeles. segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: And I go in there. And of course, it's just like a crummy Korean restaurant. It's not that clean. And I don't know-- there are tanks and stuff, but I didn't know what to order. So I order a fish soup, because it looks like they have a small fish soup specialty on the menu. And it comes, and it's just really strong-smelling, not that great. segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: And I'm about to give up, and pay the check, and go home with a vast table filled with uneaten stuff. And it suddenly occurs to me what the specialty of the restaurant is. And I wave the waitress over, and I tell her that I'd like a prawn. And she is puzzled. She didn't expect me to ask for a prawn. But I repeat my request, and she shrugs, and goes, and tells the sushi chef.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: And he goes to one side of the restaurant. He climbs on this chair, this ordinary folding chair, and he reaches into this long tank that's running just below the ceiling. And he picks out a couple of the liveliest ones and brings them back to his counter, and-- without washing his hands, mind you-- just makes a few motions over it. segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: Now, what he'd done is he'd taken off the exoskeleton. He'd essentially-- the head was intact. And that little part of the tail that is always on prawns is still there. segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: And that was a really freakish moment, because as much stuff as I eat, and as low as I eat on the food chain, and as many prawns as I have dispatched in my life, I have never before killed a living being with my teeth. segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: And I wasn't quite sure what to do. But if I put it down, the prawn would have died anyway. segments.speaker: Jonathan Gold
segments.text: And the taste of the prawn, the taste of the meat of it was extraordinary. It was sweet. It was like there was life coursing through it. segments.text: When you bit into the prawn, did you actually bite off its head, its living head, and have its head and its eyes in your mouth?

segments.text: Did you feel like there was something about the experience that made it more-- this word is a little cornier than I intend, but it's the only word that I can think of-- that made it more sacred, that took it out of the mundaneness of the way that we eat, which, for most of us, is eating without actually tasting, and experiencing, and thinking about what we're eating, and what on the Earth it is that we're killing to survive?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Howard Chackowicz and I have been friends since we're kids. And so I can say with great authority that almost every day for the past 10 years, Howard Chackowicz has either dined out or ordered in at least one of his meals.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Sometimes, when Howard isn't sure what he's in the mood for, he'll lift an empty hand up to his mouth and pretend that he's eating. He stares straight ahead, trying to figure out if he likes the taste of the imaginary food he's shoving into his mouth. Sometimes, his hand is holding a hamburger. Sometimes, a fork wrapped in spaghetti. And other times, he is double-fisting either end of an invisible pork rib.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Howard's always loved restaurants. He was raised in a Jewish Eastern-European household, where the very idea of a restaurant was a ridiculous piece of decadence, something for Cossacks and cocaine addicts who enjoyed flushing their money down the toilet. Restaurants had a transgressive allure. And as soon as Howard was old enough, he started sneaking away to them after school or sometimes on weekends while the whole family was still asleep.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: In fact, Howard was the very first person I've ever dined out with alone, without any family. We were 12 years old, and we ate at Atomics Pizzeria, a place just down the street from us. It was owned by a crotchety old Greek man named Costa, who served ridiculously large portions of food.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: We'd get a plate of fries the size of a dead Shetland pony. But right alongside of it, Costa would place one measly packet of ketchup. When we asked for more, he looked at us like we had just asked for more blood from his mother's still beating heart. Whereas I learned to ration, eating 400 to 500 French fries with a bottle-cap-sized dollop, Howard learned how to talk to Costa, how to win him over, how to make him see that giving us more ketchup was just the right thing to do.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Along the way, Howard learned how to say in Greek, thank you, kind sir, bless you for the ketchup, as well as the excellent [SPEAKING GREEK] ketchup sauce-- here's many years to your ketchup.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Ever since way back then, Howard has had a very special rapport with the men and women of the food service industry. And he has worked very hard over the years to cultivate this relationship.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: This is my neighborhood here. I've been to every single restaurant in this neighborhood several times, so I feel like I can call in on every restaurant.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: A couple of weeks ago, Howard took me on a walking tour of the best places to eat in his neighborhood. I've walked into bakeries with Howard where the young girls and old men alike who work there have dropped their doughnut tongs to cry out with joy, Howard! I've watched him get moved to the front of the line outside restaurants in Chinatown.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: When he's relating to a waiter or a deliveryman, all that Howard sees is one person giving another person food. He talks to them as though they are friends-- brothers, even. His servers are able to sense his purity of vision, and they bestow on him, in every exchange, some little bit of special treatment.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Well, let me just show you a ghost here. On the corner there is a place called-- I'm not sure what that is. That used to be called Le Defi, which is The Challenge. And that was a really great place. And then they closed and they moved right across the street. And they had $1.99 spaghetti meal. I would go there every day, and I brought a lot of friends. But I got so-- it got to the point where, when I came in, I was actually able to serve myself.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: That's how close we got. We'd go in. They'd greet me, and they wouldn't even get up. I would go, and I would pour myself coffee. And I would actually serve other people coffee. segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: In fact, Howard is such a beloved figure in the neighborhood that whenever our friend, Tucker, goes into get takeout from Sarah's, a local Middle Eastern restaurant, he'll tell whoever is serving him that, in fact, the food was not for him, but that he was picking it up for Howard. This earned him portions that were almost twice as large as what he'd normally get. Howard, he is the best man, his server would say, as he piled food onto his plate. You are so lucky to have a friend like Howard. Indeed, he was.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: But the funny thing is is that Howard is so doted upon when he eats in restaurants that sometimes, it makes it difficult for him to just sit back and enjoy his meal. He feels he has to balance things out, and so he dotes right back. Because of that, it could be hard to carry on a conversation with him. His eyes will nervously scan the restaurant for any way he could be of help to the waiting staff. Howard's ears can detect the muted clink of cutlery falling to the carpet from clear across the room. And when he does, he'll do a kind of concerned gym-coach trot over to the mishandled piece of silverware and pluck it up off the floor.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: So as much as Howard loves restaurants, when he really wants to relax, he'll get home delivery. And since it was nearing lunchtime, rather than step into one of the many restaurants we were passing, Howard ushered us back in the direction of his house to dial out for our grub. At his place, he pulled open his top kitchen drawer, and I saw the many choices that lay before us.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: There's about 400 menus in that drawer.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: I wouldn't say it's 400. I'd love to count it.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Just give me an idea.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: I'd say if this handful is about 10-- 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70--

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: As much as restaurant owners and waiters love Howard, it's delivery men who really, really love him. Who among us even knows our delivery man's name? Howard knows their names and the names of their wives and children. When they come to his door, he invites them in and offers them water. And in return, they'll actually call Howard later on to see if his meal was to his liking, that it was warm enough, that there was enough ketchup.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: --190, 200-- this is very embarrassing-- 210, 220, 230, about 250 menus in here. There are some doubles, for sure, or even like multiple copies, but only restaurants I order from all the time.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: We decide to order from Howard's favorite restaurant, a souvlaki place called The Greek Village.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: I'm going to take a number 10, the two-gyro pizza. And I think that's it Thanks. Have a nice day. Bye.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: While we wait for the food, Howard waves me over and opens his kitchen cupboard to reveal physical proof of his good standing with the service industry.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Here we go. These are all bags of ketchup, salt, soy sauce.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And this is all from takeout.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And these are big bags full of nothing but ketchup.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: There's some soy sauce.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: So gone are the days where you had to wheedle out a single packet out of Costa's hands for your French fries.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: It's true that I have so much now, I have so many packets here. But no matter how many packets I amass, it'll never catch up to what I missed as a child, ketchup.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: [KNOCKING]

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Then, with vaudeville timing, our delivery arrives.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Hey, Shamir.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Howard greets the delivery man like an old friend he hasn't seen in quite some time.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Thanks so much, man.

segments.speaker: Shamir
segments.text: He's your friend. He's a beautiful man. He's such a nice man, I'm telling you.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: I didn't get you in trouble, though.

segments.speaker: Shamir
segments.text: He's the best customer in Montreal I have.

segments.speaker: Shamir
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Shamir
segments.text: Each time I come, he gave me apple. He give me a juice. He give me everything.

segments.speaker: Shamir
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: When I order in, like most people, I figure these guys want out of my house as badly as a bird that's accidentally flown in down the chimney. And I assist them in their passage, usually having the exact change with a tip all ready for them at the door. But at Howard's house, delivery men stay a long time. They seem to want to.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Shamir, can if I offer you something?

segments.speaker: Shamir
segments.text: No, thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Hey, so Marvin's not working there anymore?

segments.speaker: Shamir
segments.text: No, because I think he find somewhere else a job.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Oh, OK. OK. I see everything is different. Actually, I felt so bad when I called, because when I ask, I say, Shamir, you know. They're like, well, we don't know who you're going to get.

segments.speaker: Shamir
segments.text: Oh, you don't have to feel bad.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: I know, but I don't want to get you in trouble.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: After about 10 minutes of this, I just want to eat. I find myself eyeing the bag of souvlaki lying on the floor like a campground bear. I realize then that I'm just not made of the same stuff as Howard, and I never will be.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When we finally sit down to eat, I can't even get Howard to admit that he's doing anything so special with guys like Shamir. We go back and forth on this.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Yeah, because most people won't go to the extent that you do, which is why you have guys that work the telephone coming by your house to meet you. That probably doesn't happen that often.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Well, I really believe I don't really do anything. I'm nice to them.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: But just empirically, you have to see at this point that you're getting responded to differently than most people, so there must be something different, no?

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: If someone's going to come to my door more than a few times, and they know my face, and we're saying, how are you, I'm going to start treating that person like a human being. And most people, I think, are probably rude to them. Most people that I know give deliveryman a buck. And I think that they do a hard-- they have a harder job than a waiter or a waitress because here's a guy who takes your food, gets into a car, risks his life, goes into traffic--

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Hang on a second? Risks his life?

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: Oh he's driving a car, you know?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Howard's worked all kinds of food service jobs himself-- as a waiter, a busboy, a short-order cook. And he says that as a result, he absolutely loathes the feeling of being served. There's something that just feels embarrassing and unnatural about it.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: But it even goes further than that. In his interactions with the service industry, he's looking for a particular feeling, a kind of cozy moment where he can palpably sense that the waiter has forgotten that he is a waiter and that they are both simply relating as human beings. And then once he knows this, once he knows they're both getting along and everyone's happy, he can move on. He isn't looking for anything else from them. His motives are pure that way.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: But these kinds of special moments don't come without strings attached. And sometimes, Howard gets into trouble. Earlier in the day, during our walking tour, there was one place we didn't stop into, a little convenience store around the corner. Howard became uncharacteristically somber and quiet as we walked by the storefront window.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: The owners, a Greek woman in her 60s named Voula and her older sister, used to be pretty friendly with him. Sometimes, Voula wouldn't charge him the tax on his chocolate bar. And on occasion, she'd have him sit behind the counter with her on a plastic milk crate. It wasn't much, but it was still more than what the other customers got. And it made Howard feel special. But then, at a certain point, things started to get more intense.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: There had been several holdups there, by knifepoint, gunpoint. And I felt really bad for them. I'd see them really shook up. And they're kind of tough ladies, but they're alone. And I told them, I said, if you ever need anything, if there's any trouble or something, I'm just around the corner. You give me a call. And I really meant it like in case of emergency or just that there'd be someone they can call, some kind of community, some type of effort at community. But she started-- she would call every day.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: She would call him for all kinds of reasons, to have him come by and fix things or to run errands for her. And he would try his best to be accommodating. She'd even call him just to chat.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Even though all of this was more than Howard could shoulder, he was reluctant to put an end to it. It was only after the calls got later into the night, at 1:00 and 2:00 in the morning, that Howard's friends started insisting he tell her that enough was enough. And against his better judgment, he did so. Howard wonders if it was right to give her his number in the first place.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: I made that offer assuming that it would be understood that there's a cutoff point. But to another person, that offer is a real, genuine offer. If I need help, I'm going to call you, and she did. And maybe she's the one that's right.

segments.speaker: Howard Chackowicz
segments.text: So it's ironic that being nice to someone actually had the adverse effect, the opposite effect, and it ended up being a disaster. And now, two people are not even friendly with each other.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: There have been other disasters for Howard, disasters where he was the one who went a little too far. Like there's the time he became so consumed with helping this neighborhood Chinese restaurant that, without being asked, he took it upon himself to draw up pamphlets for the place. The owner accepted Howard's flyers, but never circulated them. Later, the owner picked a screaming fight with Howard over an order, and Howard never went back.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And then there was the time he brought in beautiful framed photos of Lebanon to his favorite Lebanese restaurant so they could be reminded of home. But the photos were never hung up, nor were they ever referred to again.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: But for Howard, those things don't matter, and I know that he'd probably even do them all again. There are so many other moments that make his good intentions feel repaid in full. Some of his favorites are when deliverymen he knows pass him by in their cars as he's walking down the street. It shocks him out of his reverie when they honk their horns in a quick, affectionate burst. For a brief moment, it feels like a reassuring slap on the back. Howard thinks to himself that they're the best, and it fills him with so much gratitude that if he had a pear or a peach in his coat pocket, he would wave them over and give it to them.
